title: Signals and Systems in Discrete Time

contract.reader: An engineering student or engineer with calculus, complex numbers and the idea of sampling, starting the DSP series with samples already in memory
contract.problem: Knowing what frequency means for a sequence and which systems can be analyzed, and describing such a system by a difference equation and an impulse response
contract.outcome: Convert hertz to radians per sample and explain discrete-time aliasing; test linearity, time invariance, causality, memory and BIBO stability; run a difference equation in the series' sign convention; convolve by hand; read causality, stability and DC gain from h[n]; compute a first frequency response
contract.contribution: One compact path from sequences to frequency response that fixes the notation and sign conventions of the whole series, with two running examples (moving average, exponential smoother), a mains-interference example and two scripts with output
contract.evidence: Derivations in the text; two Python/NumPy scripts with output; Oppenheim and Schafer (2010), Oppenheim, Willsky and Nawab (1997), Proakis and Manolakis (2007)
contract.limitations: No z-transform, DFT, filter design or finite word length (later entries); sample values treated as unquantized

findings.location: Section 6.2 derivation of H (1280 and 360 px); at 360 px also Sections 2.2, 3.1, 4.2, 6.1 and 6.3 display equations
findings.problem: Display equations are wider than the column and scroll sideways with no cue; at 1280 px the 6.2 result (1 + 2cos w)e^{-jw} is hidden, at 360 px most central equations show only their left part
findings.whyItMatters: These are the results the sections derive (difference-equation convention, convolution sum, frequency response, the mains-rejecting zero); readers see incomplete formulas where the argument depends on them
findings.action: Break the long equations over lines (aligned blocks; one form per line for 3.1 and 4.2)
findings.acceptance: On new captures the 6.2 equation is fully visible at 1280 px and no line of the listed equations is cut at 360 px, light and dark

findings.problem: The question asks how many samples the step response takes to reach 95%; the answer gives the index n = 59 (the 60th sample)
findings.whyItMatters: A reader who counts samples answers 60 and thinks they are wrong
findings.action: Ask for the index, or give both index and count in the answer
